title: How to retouch product photos for e‑commerce
summary: Learn how to retouch e‑commerce photos with simple tools and techniques. Create clean, professional images to showcase your products effectively.
body_markdown:
Even a well-planned product shoot can result in visuals with dust, inaccurate color, fabric wrinkles, distracting reflections, or an unwanted object in the frame. Retouching addresses those problems before the image reaches your marketplace listing or online store.


This work once meant spending hours in desktop editing software or paying a service for each image. Photoroom gives sellers more direct ways to handle routine corrections, from localized cleanup and wrinkle reduction to backgrounds, shadows, and resizing.


The goal is not to make the product look perfect. Good retouching removes distractions caused by the shoot and presents the item clearly without changing its real color, texture, condition, construction, or features. If the photo is blurred, severely overexposed, missing important details, or poorly composed, a reshoot is usually more reliable than aggressive editing.


## What is product photo retouching?


Photo retouching is the act of editing or manipulating a digital image to improve it visually, adjust its technical qualities, or both.


For product photography, retouching usually means correcting specific imperfections or refining product details. Common examples include removing dust, cleaning edges, balancing color,[reducing distracting wrinkles](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/best-AI-tools-to-iron-clothes-in-photos) , and refining shadows or reflections. Retouching’s purpose is to improve clarity and presentation without misrepresenting the product.


Retouching overlaps with basic photo editing, but they aren’t identical.[A listing-ready workflow](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-listing) may include editing, retouching, and transformation:


Task type What it changes E‑commerce examples


Basic editing The overall image, composition, or output Cropping, exposure, resizing, aspect ratio, and file format


Retouching A localized error or product-specific detail Dust removal, color correction, wrinkle reduction, and reflection cleanup


Transformation The scene or represented variant A new background, another colorway, or a new composition


Transformations need additional scrutiny because they can affect product accuracy or marketplace eligibility. A generated lifestyle background can work well for a secondary image or ad, but not for a marketplace that requires a plain background for a primary listing image.

Small, isolated corrections against simple surroundings are generally easier to review. Intricate labels, patterns, transparent edges, reflective surfaces, and fine textures require closer attention. When an edit changes a product fact instead of correcting the photograph, undo it, try a more controlled method, or reshoot the product.


## What to know about retouching photos for stronger results


Retouching a product listing becomes easier when e‑commerce sellers start with high quality photographs, organize their photoshoot with editing in mind, and understand the limitations of retouching. These tips can help prevent poorly edited images or eventual reshoots.


### 1. Start with a clear, high-quality source photo


Retouching works best when the original photo is sharp, well-lit, and provides enough accurate information to work with. Low-resolution, blurry or pixelated images are hard to fix, and some will need a reshoot. Reshoot if the focus is off or if labels, patterns or surface textures aren’t legible. Those details have to match the real product.


### 2. Get lighting and exposure right during the shoot


If an image is too dark or overexposed, retouching can help but with limited improvements. Aim to capture photos in natural or consistent lighting to reduce post-production work and make color easier to compare across products.


Pay particular attention to bright reflective areas. When highlights are clipped to pure white, there may not be enough surface detail left to recover.


### 3. Use a simple background


Replacing an inconsistent background and preserving clean product edges becomes harder with a complex or busy background. For more reliable results with background removal and replacement, shoot against a plain background.


A simple setup also reduces the risk of background colors reflecting onto the product and changing its photographed color.


### 4. Be realistic about object removal


Removing an unwanted item from a background is easier when it’s surrounded by a solid, uniform area. Heavy clutter, uneven shadows, patterned surfaces, and overlap with the product can complicate the result. Work in multiple small passes around edges, text, labels, and patterns rather than making one broad selection. This gives you more control over the area being reconstructed.


### 5. Know what shouldn’t or can’t be fixed


Remove artifacts introduced by the shoot, such as dust, lint, a stray prop, or a temporary color cast. Preserve real product characteristics, including natural texture, construction details, wear, condition, seams, and defects a customer needs to see.


For example, removing a used item’s permanent scratch would misrepresent its condition. For a leather bag, smoothing away the grain would change how the material appears. Accuracy matters more than surface perfection.


## How to retouch a photo with Photoroom


[Photoroom’s AI Retouch tool](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/remove-object-from-photo) can clean up isolated distractions such as dust, lint, props, or small reflections.


Here's the step-by-step process.


### 1. Open Retouch in the Photoroom app


Go to the Photoroom web or mobile app. On web, scroll through the options under Get Started and select Retouch an image. You can also find Retouch under See all tools, in the photo editor, or by searching for it.


On mobile, Retouch is located under AI tools → Editing tools.


### 2. Upload your image


Select an image from your computer or mobile phone, or start from a previous upload or design.


###


### 3. Set the brush size


Drag the slider to choose a brush size. Use a larger brush for an isolated object surrounded by a simple background. Switch to a smaller brush when working near the product, a label, a pattern, or a detailed edge.


###


### 4. Brush over the unwanted area


Brush over the object, dust, or reflection you want to remove, focusing only on the area you want erased. Don’t cover more of the surrounding product than necessary.


Use smaller passes near fine details. If a distraction crosses the product edge, consider cleaning the background side and product side separately so you can inspect each reconstruction.


###


### 5. Review the reconstructed area


Inspect the result at higher zoom. Look for smearing, repeated texture, bent edges, missing details, or an area that no longer matches the surrounding material.


If part of the distraction remains, try another smaller pass. If the edit changes text, logos, seams, surface texture, shape, or another product fact, undo the result. A reshoot may be safer when the unwanted element covers critical details.


###


### 6. Make listing-ready adjustments


Once the localized cleanup is complete, prepare the whole image for its intended channel:


1.


Clean any remaining dust or small distractions.


2.


Correct other product-specific issues using[Edit with AI](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/edit-with-ai) ,[Product Beautifier](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-beautifier) , or[Wrinkle Remover](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/remove-wrinkles-clothes) .


3.


Standardize the setting with[Background Remover](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) or[White Background](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/white-background) .


4.


Use[AI Backgrounds](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/instant-backgrounds) for eligible secondary or marketing images.


5.


If needed, add or refine a shadow with[AI Shadows](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/instant-shadows) .


6.


Use[Image Resizer](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/image-resizer) to meet the channel’s dimensions and aspect ratio.


7.


Use[AI Expand](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/ai-expand) when you need to make the image taller or wider for another platform.


8.


Use[AI Image Enhancer](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/photo-enhancer) when better output quality would be useful. But remember: enhancement can’t recover missing product facts.


### 7. Export and compare with the original product


Export the finished image.


Before publishing it to your marketplace, listing, or social media channel, compare it with both the original source photo and the physical item. Make sure the cleanup did not change the product’s color, shape, texture, labels, condition, or included components.[Photoroom’s AI Product Fixer](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-fixer) automatically detects errors in AI-generated edits, and allows you to correct discrepancies without using additional credits. This is part of[Photoroom’s product fidelity layer](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/introducing-photoroom-fidelity-layer-for-image-editing) , and it’s embedded into every tool.


## How to handle common photo retouching problems


Object removal is only one part of e‑commerce retouching. Color, clothing, reflections, backgrounds, and shadows may each need different edits and accuracy checks.


### How to correct product color without misleading buyers


Color correction means making a photograph match the physical item. This is necessary when a camera, lighting, or white balance causes the color to shift during the image creation process. Recoloring means creating an image of a different product variant. They’re separate tasks.


When color correcting, compare the image with the physical product under neutral, consistent light. Check the product on more than one screen where possible because displays render color differently. The end goal is to make the listing a trustworthy representation of what customers will receive.


Use particular caution with metallic, translucent, iridescent, glossy, and multi-material products. Their appearance changes with lighting and viewing angle, so an aggressive correction can make the image less accurate to real life. If you can’t produce a trustworthy result from the original file, reshoot with more controlled lighting.


[Recolor clothing](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) when you need to showcase another available colorway without reshooting the product. Review the recolored image carefully, especially around patterns, stitching, trims, buttons, logos, and materials that should not change. Don’t use recoloring to cover up an inaccurate source photo or create a variant you don’t actually sell.


Accurate color helps set reliable customer expectations. It doesn’t guarantee fewer returns, but it reduces one avoidable source of mismatch between a listing and the delivered item.


### How to remove wrinkles without changing the garment


[Removing wrinkles](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/remove-wrinkles-clothes) should clean up distracting storage or handling creases without erasing the garment’s construction, texture, or natural drape. Natural folds can help customers understand fit, thickness, and fabric behavior. Removing every fold may make the garment look artificial or structurally different.


A practical clothing workflow is:


1.


Open Photoroom and select See all tools.


2.


Under Refine your product shots, select Ironing.


3.


Upload your image and the tool automatically reduces distracting creases.


4.


Inspect collars, cuffs, seams, hems, logos, prints, and patterned areas.


5.


Confirm that the garment’s texture, shape, drape, and construction remain accurate.


6.


If genuine features have changed, undo the result or use a specialist.


### How to reduce reflections and glare


Not every reflection is a flaw. Highlights and reflections often communicate the curvature and finish of glass, polished metal, jewelry, and glossy packaging. Removing them all can flatten the object or make its material harder to understand.


Small, distracting reflections may be suitable for[AI Retouch](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/remove-object-from-photo) or a carefully tested[Edit with AI](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/edit-with-ai) request.


Afterward, inspect labels, edges, text, and surface texture for changes.


Large blown out highlights are different. If the camera didn’t record any detail in the bright area, an editor can’t reliably recover what the product looked like beneath it. Instead of undergoing excessive retouching, reflective products often benefit more from changing the camera angle, diffusing the light, or reshooting.


### How to clean backgrounds and keep shadows realistic


Use[Background Remover](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) when the original setting is distracting or inconsistent. Use[White Background](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/white-background) when a clean white image suits the marketplace, category, and image position.


[AI Backgrounds](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/instant-shadows) is more appropriate for permitted secondary listing images, ads, social posts, or other contextual visuals. Generated settings should still make physical sense for the product, and they may not meet the rules for a marketplace’s primary image.


After changing the background,[AI Shadows](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/instant-shadows) can make the product appear more naturally in the frame. Review the shadow’s direction, softness, size, and contact point. A shadow that conflicts with the product’s highlights or appears disconnected from its base will make the visual less credible.


Broader cleanup tools can also fit this process. Use Edit with AI to make changes with custom prompts, and use[Product Beautifier](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-beautifier) to apply studio-quality edits (enhance lighting, boost quality, and sharpen color) all at once. Like with any generative AI tool, check the final output against the original image, and verify that important details such as color, text, shape, and hardware haven’t changed.


## How to keep retouching consistent across a catalog


Consistency isn’t simply making every image look polished. It means applying the same visual rules so shoppers can compare products without differences in crop, background, scale, or color getting in the way.


For consistent catalog imagery, start by creating an approved reference image that defines:


-


Canvas dimensions and aspect ratio


-


Product position and apparent scale


-


Crop and margins


-


Background treatment


-


Shadow direction and softness


-


White balance and color rendering


-


Acceptable degree of cleanup


-


Export dimensions and file type


Then correct and approve one representative image before applying the treatment to the rest of the catalog. Choose a product with typical edges, materials, and details—not just the easiest item to edit. Keep the physical item or another reliable reference available when approving color.


For multiple images,[Batch Mode](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) can apply supported, repeatable work such as background, positioning, and formatting changes. In Photoroom, you can[save these edits as a template](https://www.photoroom.com/templates) that can be reapplied across multiple images. Batch edit images only after establishing the standard on one approved image; otherwise, you risk repeating the wrong treatment across the catalog.


Automated treatments can also produce outliers. Transparent objects, reflective packaging, fine hair or fabric edges, unusually shaped products, or complex patterns may need individual attention.


Finally, review the images as a collection rather than approving them one at a time. Compare apparent product scale, margins, alignment, background color, shadows, white balance, cleanup intensity, and variant accuracy.


For a more in-depth look at when to move beyond one-by-one editing, read[Scaling product photos: manual vs automation explained](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/scaling-product-photos) .


## Should you use AI, edit manually, hire a service, or reshoot?


The right option depends on the defect, the number of images, and how costly an inaccurate result would be.


**Option**


**Best for**


**Limitations**


AI-assisted e‑commerce tool


Routine cleanup, backgrounds, shadows, clothing wrinkles, sizing, and repeatable listing preparation


Requires review and may change text, patterns, edges, color, or details


Manual editor


Precise masks, controlled compositing, complex texture repair, and difficult edge work


Higher learning curve and slower one-by-one workflow


Retouching professional or service


High-value hero images, jewelry, beauty products, reflective materials, major reconstruction, or exact art direction


Higher cost and more handoff time


Reshoot


Blur, missing details, severe clipping, poor angles, inaccurate source color, or weak composition


Requires access to the product and another shoot


Use AI when the issue is routine, limited, and easy to verify. Manual editing or professional help makes more sense when small precision errors would be expensive or difficult to spot. Reshoot when essential visual information is absent.


Human review matters because generated edits can alter product details.[In Photoroom’s own benchmark of four general-purpose image-editing models](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/top-editing-image-models-maintain-product-details-only-28-of-the-time) across 850 products, the tested models passed only 14%–28% of the benchmark’s product-fidelity checks. Common failure modes included distorted logos and text, missing or changed elements, altered patterns, and color shifts.


Photoroom is designed around[e‑commerce product-image workflows](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-repeatable-product-image-workflow) , making it a practical choice for common cleanup and listing preparation. It’s not a replacement for every specialist retouching task or a better source photo.


## How much photo retouching is too much?


A reasonable edit removes artifacts caused by the shoot, corrects differences between the photograph and the physical item, and improves presentation without changing product facts.


An edit has gone too far when it:


-


Hides damage or condition relevant to the buyer


-


Changes the material, shape, fit, or construction


-


Creates a color or variant that is not sold


-


Removes labels, seams, texture, or included features


-


Invents details that weren’t originally captured


-


Makes the image ineligible for its intended marketplace role


Use the physical product as the final standard. Retouching is misleading when the image makes a promise the item can’t keep.


Marketplace requirements also depend on the platform, category, and image position. Primary listing images often have stricter rules for backgrounds, composition, props, text, and product visibility. Secondary images may allow lifestyle settings or generated backgrounds.


Check the current requirements for each destination rather than relying on one universal standard. A visual suitable for your online store or social feed might not qualify as the main image on a marketplace.


## How to review product photos for quality control: a checklist


Before publishing an edited image, check:


-


Does the image still match the physical product?


-


Are the color, texture, shape, and condition accurate?


-


Are logos, labels, text, prints, seams, and edges intact?


-


Did cleanup introduce blur, repeated texture, or invented details?


-


Are genuine material reflections still present where needed?


-


Are the shadows plausible and consistent?


-


Is the background appropriate for the marketplace and image position?


-


Are crop, product scale, margins, and alignment consistent?


-


Is the product clear at marketplace-thumbnail size?


-


Does the file meet current dimension and format requirements?


-


Have alternate-color images been checked against variants that are actually available?


## Retouch product photos in a complete workflow with Photoroom


Product photo retouching works best as a controlled finishing process: start with an accurate photo, correct only what needs attention, prepare it for the intended channel, and review the result against the real product.


Photoroom supports seller workflows including localized cleanup, clothing wrinkle reduction, background preparation, shadows, resizing, and repeatable catalog editing.
